You compare cities and places, say what is “the most…”, and use -ísimo and “tan / tanto como”.
Madrid is the biggest city in Spain.
This restaurant is the best in the neighbourhood.
The paella is really, really good.
Barcelona is as beautiful as Madrid.
To form the superlative: el más alto de…, la mejor de…
To compare with tan… como and tanto(s)… como.
To say “more than 100”: más de cien.
To recommend places and give your opinion about a city.
Tom, Ana and Mihai argue about which is the most beautiful city in Spain.
For me, Barcelona is the most beautiful city in Spain.
I disagree! Madrid is as beautiful as Barcelona. And it has the best museums in the country.
But Barcelona has a beach. And Gaudí’s architecture is incredibly original.
That’s true. The Sagrada Familia is the most impressive monument I’ve ever seen.
Ha, ha. Madrid is bigger, but Barcelona is less noisy.
Madrid has over three million inhabitants. Barcelona, under two.
But Madrid’s nightlife is the best in the world. Nobody sleeps here!
That’s true. And the food… your mother’s cocido is amazing.
OK, OK. And Bucharest, Mihai? How does it compare with Madrid?
Bucharest isn’t as big, but it has as many parks as Madrid. And the people are just as nice.
And the Palace of the Parliament is the heaviest building in the world, isn’t it?
Yes! Well… they all have something special! You have to visit them all.
The stress always falls on the “Í”: bwe-NÍ-si-mo, ka-RÍ-si-mo, gran-DÍ-si-mo. Say it with enthusiasm!
Review the harsh j in “mejor”, the hard g in “Gaudí” and “edificio” (c = th).
Spaniards link vowels between words: “la ciudad más alta” = “laciudadmásalta”. “Es el” = “esel”.
The formula: ARTICLE + (noun) + MÁS / MENOS + adjective + DE + group.
He’s the tallest boy in the class.
It’s the least expensive neighbourhood in the city.
Watch the “DE”: “el más alto DE la clase” (in the class). Not “en la clase”, even though English says “in”. And the article agrees: EL chico, LA ciudad, LOS museos.
The irregular forms: el mejor (the best), el peor (the worst), el mayor (the oldest), el menor (the youngest).
It’s the best restaurant in the neighbourhood.
To say “extremely”, you add -ísimo / -ísima to the adjective. It’s very common in speech, more expressive than “muy”.
The rule: if the adjective ends in a vowel, drop it and add -ísimo (bueno → buen + ísimo). If it ends in a consonant, add it directly (fácil → facilísimo).
3. Equality: tan… como and tanto… como
“Tanto” agrees with the noun: tanto dinero, tanta gente, tantos parques, tantas playas. “Tan” never changes.
And “igual de… que” or “igual que”: Es igual de simpática que tú. Hablo igual que mi madre.
When you compare with a number, you use “más de” / “menos de”, NOT “más que”:
Madrid has over three million inhabitants.
It costs less than ten euros.
“Más que” is for comparing two things; “más de” is for numbers: Tengo más de 30 años, but Soy más alto que tú.
5. How to give your opinion and recommend
Lo mejor de… es… / Lo peor de… es…
The best thing about… is… / The worst thing…
“Lo mejor” = the best part: “Lo mejor de Madrid es la gente” = The best thing about Madrid is the people.
el chico más alto de la clase
el chico más alto en la clase
el más chico alto de la clase

A short travel guide written by Carmen, Lucía’s friend, who lives in Seville.
Seville is the capital of Andalusia and, for me, the liveliest city in Spain.
It has almost seven hundred thousand inhabitants: it isn’t as big as Madrid, but it’s full of life.
The most famous monument is the cathedral. It’s one of the biggest cathedrals in the world.
Next to it is the Giralda, a very old tower. From the top, the view is spectacular.
The Alcázar is, in my opinion, the most beautiful place in the city. Its gardens are extraordinarily beautiful.
The worst thing about Seville is the heat: in August it’s over forty-five degrees.
That’s why the best time to visit is spring.
In April there’s the Feria: a week of flamenco, colourful dresses and partying day and night.
I recommend the Triana neighbourhood. That’s where the most authentic tapas bars are.
Tapas are really cheap: a tapa costs less than three euros.
And the people are as friendly as they say. It’s worth a visit!

Every October, the La Latina neighbourhood holds a tapas competition. This year Kenji decided to take part.
There were twenty bars in the competition. For a week, customers tried the tapas and voted for the best one.
The favourite was Paco’s bar, the oldest in the neighbourhood. His croquette tapa had won for the last five years.
Kenji wanted to do something different: a tapa that mixed Japanese and Spanish cooking.
He tried lots of ideas. The first was sushi with jamón, but it was too salty.
The second was a tortilla with wasabi. Mihai tried it and said it was the spiciest thing he had ever eaten.
In the end Kenji invented the “cocido gyoza”: a Japanese dumpling filled with Grandma Rosario’s cocido.
It was less traditional than Paco’s croquettes, but much more original.
On the first evening only ten customers came. On the second, fifty came.
On Thursday a newspaper wrote: “The most surprising tapa in Madrid”. By Friday there were queues in the street.
On Sunday they announced the results. Paco’s croquettes came second. Kenji’s gyoza won with over a thousand votes.
Kenji was nervous: he didn’t know how Paco would react.
But Paco came over, shook his hand and said: “It’s the best tapa I’ve tasted in forty years. Next year I’ll beat you.”
And Grandma Rosario, very proud, told everyone: “The cocido recipe is mine.”
The following year the two bars teamed up for the competition. Together they presented a new tapa: ramen croquettes. They won, of course.
And on the wall of Kenji’s bar, next to the certificate, there is now a photo of Paco and Kenji hugging.
